explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, the Philistines. David defeats them, subdues them, and takes Gath and its villages from their hand. The chapter opens with a win and doesn't slow down. I'm still catching my breath, and I only read it.

Egypt is a big name, so I get why it came to mind. But these verses never mention the Egyptians. The first people David defeats and subdues are the Philistines. Egypt would have made the chapter even longer, and it's already a sprint.

The Assyrians sound like they belong in a war chapter, don't they? But this passage never names them. It opens with David defeating and subduing the Philistines and taking Gath and its villages. The names get packed in fast here, so keep your eyes open.

explanations.answer: They serve David and bring tribute
explanations.explanation: That's it. The Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute. The text says they became subject to him, so this wasn't a fifty-fifty deal. Think of a gift basket you didn't ask for, only with a king on the receiving end.

explanations.answer: They flee and leave their land
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say the Moabites ran off anywhere. It says they became subject to David and brought him tribute. So they stayed put and started sending payments. That's a long way from packing the moving truck.

explanations.answer: They join David as equal partners
explanations.explanation: Equal partners sounds friendly, but that isn't how the verse puts it. The Moabites became subject to David, and they brought him tribute. Subject means under him, not beside him. Nobody gets a shared office with a name plate in that arrangement.

Close, but no cookie for this one. David doesn't keep every horse. He keeps a hundred for the chariots, and he hamstrings all the rest of them (1 Chronicles 18:4). A thousand chariots is a lot to take, and the text still says only a hundred horses are kept.

Right, friend. David captures a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers and twenty thousand foot soldiers. But he hamstrings all the horses except a hundred that he keeps for the chariots. The text tells us what he does and doesn't give a reason, so I'll leave it there.

Yes! David places garrisons in Aram of Damascus. A garrison is a group of soldiers stationed in a place, so the land stays under his hand. After that, the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute.

explanations.answer: A king to rule for him
explanations.explanation: A stand-in king would be a neat idea, but the verse doesn't mention one. What David places there are garrisons, which are troops stationed in the land. Then the Arameans become subject to him and bring tribute. No crown gets handed out in this verse.

No altar gets built in Aram of Damascus in this passage. David places garrisons there, meaning troops. David does give something to the LORD later in the chapter, when he dedicates the silver and gold he has carried off (1 Chronicles 18:11). That's a different moment, so hold onto that thought.

The LORD! The chapter says it plainly: "So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went." Look at all the battles packed in here, and the writer still stops to say who is behind them. I like a chapter that gives credit where it's due.

David does have an army, and the chapter even lists his army's commander later. But the verse doesn't credit the army. It says, "So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went." The writer wants us to know who is behind every win.

David's people show up later in the chapter, when he administers justice and righteousness for all his people (1 Chronicles 18:14). But the victory line points somewhere else. The verse says, "So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went." The credit goes to the LORD.

Solomon, David's son and the king who comes after him. The passage says David took a large amount of bronze from Tibhath and Cun, and with it Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles. David gathers the metal, and a son uses it later. That's some serious handing down.

Absalom is one of David's sons, listed in 1 Chronicles 3:2. But the passage doesn't connect him to this bronze. It says Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles from it. Good guess on the family, though.

Adonijah is another of David's sons, listed in 1 Chronicles 3:2. Still, the verse gives the bronze job to someone else. Solomon made the bronze Sea, the pillars, and various bronze articles from it. David has a lot of sons, so I don't blame you for the mix-up.

True. Tou, king of Hamath, sends his son Hadoram to bless David for defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Tou. So David's win was good news in Hamath. I think Tou was glad somebody finally dealt with Hadadezer, but that part is only my guess.

The text says the opposite. Hadadezer had been at war with Tou, king of Hamath. That's why Tou sends his son Hadoram to greet David and bless him for defeating Hadadezer. Hadoram arrives with gold, silver and bronze, too.

Yes, friend. King David dedicated all of it to the LORD, the gifts from Hadoram and the silver and gold from all those nations. Piles of treasure, and he gives it to the LORD. I think I'd be tempted to stare at that pile awhile, so I'm impressed.

The text doesn't say anything about a new palace here. It says King David dedicated these things to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he carried off from the nations. That's a lot of treasure heading straight to the LORD.

explanations.answer: Pays the men in his army
explanations.explanation: Paying the army is a sensible idea, but the verse doesn't say it. King David dedicated the silver and gold to the LORD. The text doesn't mention a payroll at all.

Careful, because the text says more than that. After Abishai, son of Zeruiah, struck down eighteen thousand Edomites, he placed garrisons in Edom. And all the Edomites were subject to David. All of them, not just some.

False is right. The text says that all the Edomites were subject to David. Abishai, son of Zeruiah, placed garrisons in Edom after the battle in the Valley of Salt. The chapter then says again that the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.

True! The text says, "Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people." The chapter moves from battles to how David ruled. After all that fighting, it's good to see the kingdom run with justice and righteousness.

The text says the opposite. "Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people." All Israel, not part of it. The rest of the chapter lists the men who served with him.
